hints: Think about the two different types of reaction here. One reagent provides hydroxide ions that can remove the metal as an insoluble hydroxide, the other provides a high concentration of a different ligand that stays in solution.
Recall the characteristic colours of cobalt(II) species. The hydroxide precipitate and the tetrahedral chloro complex are both blue, but decide which one is a solid and which one is a solution.
walkthrough:
Sort out what each reagent does**
You start with pink $\text{[Co(H}_{2}\text{O)}_{6}\text{]}^{2+}$ in solution. With $\text{NaOH(aq)}$, the $\text{OH}^{-}$ ions act as a base and pull the cobalt out of solution as a hydroxide. With excess concentrated $\text{HCl}$, the large excess of $\text{Cl}^{-}$ ions acts as ligands and swaps into the complex, but everything stays dissolved.

Link to colour and state**
Cobalt(II) hydroxide, $\text{Co(OH)}_{2}$, is a blue precipitate, so you record colour blue and state solid. The chloro complex, $\text{[CoCl}_{4}\text{]}^{2-}$, is also blue but it is formed in solution, so you record colour blue and state aqueous.

Final answer: NaOH(aq): blue, solid / precipitate (s)
an excess of conc. HCl: blue, aqueous / solution (aq)

hints: Start with $\text{[Co(H}_{2}\text{O)}_{6}\text{]}^{2+}$ plus $\text{OH}^{-}$ and think how many hydroxide ions are needed to balance the $2+$ charge to give neutral $\text{Co(OH)}_{2}$ and free water.
walkthrough:
Build the precipitation equation**
Picture the $2+$ hexaaqua ion meeting $\text{OH}^{-}$ ions. You need two $\text{OH}^{-}$ to neutralise the $2+$ charge and form $\text{Co(OH)}_{2}$. All six water ligands are released as free $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. Check atoms and charge: $2+$ on the left from $+2$ plus $2(-1)$, zero on the right, cobalt, oxygen and hydrogen all balance to give $\text{[Co(H}_{2}\text{O)}_{6}\text{]}^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^{-} \rightarrow \text{Co(OH)}_{2} + 6\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$.

hints: This is a ligand substitution where monodentate $\text{Cl}^{-}$ replaces water. Think about the formula of the blue tetrahedral product and how many $\text{Cl}^{-}$ and $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ molecules are needed to balance ligands, atoms and charge.
walkthrough:
Build the ligand exchange equation**
Excess concentrated $\text{Cl}^{-}$ replaces all six waters to give the tetrahedral $\text{[CoCl}_{4}\text{]}^{2-}$ ion. You need four $\text{Cl}^{-}$ on the left to supply the four chloro ligands, and six $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ are released on the right. Charge balances as $+2 + 4(-1) = -2$ on both sides, giving $\text{[Co(H}_{2}\text{O)}_{6}\text{]}^{2+} + 4\text{Cl}^{-} \rightarrow \text{[CoCl}_{4}\text{]}^{2-} + 6\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$.

hints: Focus on what equilibrium the constant describes. It is not solubility or dissociation, it is the assembly step where free metal ions and ligands come together to make the complex in solution.
walkthrough:
Say exactly what equilibrium is measured**
Think of building $\text{[Co(NH}_{3}\text{)}_{6}\text{]}^{2+}$ from $\text{Co}^{2+}$ (or $\text{[Co(H}_{2}\text{O)}_{6}\text{]}^{2+}$) and $\text{NH}_{3}$. $K_{\text{stab}}$ tells you how far that formation equilibrium lies to the right. A large value means a very stable complex.
Final answer: The equilibrium constant for the formation of a complex ion from its constituent ions in solution.

hints: Write the formation equilibrium first: hexaaquacobalt(II) plus six ammonia molecules gives the hexaammine complex plus water, then apply the normal equilibrium law with products over reactants, remembering water is omitted.
walkthrough:
Apply products over reactants**
The equilibrium is $\text{[Co(H}_{2}\text{O)}_{6}\text{]}^{2+} + 6\text{NH}_{3} \rightleftharpoons \text{[Co(NH}_{3}\text{)}_{6}\text{]}^{2+} + 6\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. For $K_{\text{stab}}$ you put the complex ion concentration on top and the aqua ion concentration times the ammonia concentration raised to the power six underneath. Water is the solvent so it is left out, giving $K_{\text{stab}} = \dfrac{\text{[[Co(NH}_{3}\text{)}_{6}\text{]}^{2+}]}{\text{[[Co(H}_{2}\text{O)}_{6}\text{]}^{2+}]\text{[NH}_{3}\text{]}^{6}}$.

hints: Substitute concentration units $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ into your expression from (b)(ii) and cancel top and bottom, remembering the $\text{[NH}_{3}\text{]}^{6}$ term dominates.
walkthrough:
Cancel the concentration units**
Put $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ into $\dfrac{\text{[complex]}}{\text{[aqua][NH}_{3}\text{]}^{6}}$. The top gives $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ and the bottom gives $(\text{mol dm}^{-3}) \times (\text{mol dm}^{-3})^{6} = (\text{mol dm}^{-3})^{7}$. Dividing leaves $(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^{-6}$, which is $\text{mol}^{-6}\text{dm}^{18}$.

hints: Rearrange the $K_{\text{stab}}$ expression to make $\text{[[Co(H}_{2}\text{O)}_{6}\text{]}^{2+}]$ the subject, then substitute $K_{\text{stab}} = 7.7 \times 10^{4}$, $\text{[[Co(NH}_{3}\text{)}_{6}\text{]}^{2+}]=0.0740$ and $\text{[NH}_{3}]=0.480$ with the power of six.
walkthrough:
Rearrange and substitute**
From (b)(ii), $\text{[[Co(H}_{2}\text{O)}_{6}\text{]}^{2+}] = \dfrac{\text{[[Co(NH}_{3}\text{)}_{6}\text{]}^{2+}]}{K_{\text{stab}}\text{[NH}_{3}\text{]}^{6}}$. Put in the numbers: $$\text{[[Co(H}_{2}\text{O)}_{6}\text{]}^{2+} = \dfrac{0.0740}{(7.7 \times 10^{4}) \times (0.480)^{6}}$$ Since $(0.480)^{6} = 0.01223$, the denominator is $(7.7 \times 10^{4}) \times 0.01223 = 941.8$. So concentration $= 0.0740 / 941.8 = 7.86 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$.
